marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q001.takeaway: Trapezius paralysis weakens shoulder elevation and scapular rotation, so spinal accessory injury can produce a drooping shoulder.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q001.displayText:
Drooping of the shoulder is due to paralysis of the trapezius muscle. Trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).

Its actions include retraction of the scapula, shrugging the shoulder, and overhead abduction together with serratus anterior. Paralysis causes shoulder droop and slight winging, with prominence of the superior angle of the scapula.
emphasis: Drooping of the shoulder is due to paralysis of the trapezius muscle
Trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
Its actions include retraction of the scapula, shrugging the shoulder, and overhead abduction together with serratus anterior

rationales.b: Deltoid weakness impairs arm abduction but does not account for trapezius-mediated shoulder droop.
rationales.c: Latissimus dorsi extends/adducts/medially rotates the arm and does not elevate the shoulder girdle.
rationales.d: Serratus anterior paralysis causes medial scapular winging and impaired upward rotation rather than the classic droop from trapezius palsy.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q002.takeaway: Thoracodorsal nerve injury weakens latissimus dorsi but does not cause scapular winging; trapezius and serratus anterior are key stabilizers.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q002.displayText: The thoracodorsal nerve does not cause winging of the scapula. It supplies latissimus dorsi; injury impairs extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm.
emphasis: The thoracodorsal nerve does not cause winging of the scapula
It supplies latissimus dorsi; injury impairs extension, adduction, and medial rotation of the arm

rationales.a: Dorsal scapular nerve supplies rhomboids; injury can weaken scapular retraction and contribute to winging.
rationales.b: Spinal accessory nerve denervates trapezius and can produce shoulder droop/winging.
rationales.c: Long thoracic nerve denervates serratus anterior, producing prominent winging.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q003.takeaway: Spinal accessory injury denervates trapezius, explaining both shoulder droop and scapular winging in this shoulder-region wound.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q003.displayText:
Spinal accessory nerve injury can cause both drooping of the shoulder and winging of the scapula because it denervates trapezius.

Trapezius retracts the scapula, shrugs the shoulder, and contributes to overhead abduction with serratus anterior.
emphasis: Spinal accessory nerve injury can cause both drooping of the shoulder and winging of the scapula because it denervates trapezius
Trapezius retracts the scapula, shrugs the shoulder, and contributes to overhead abduction with serratus anterior

rationales.a: Long thoracic injury causes winging but usually not the drooping shoulder caused by loss of trapezius elevation.
rationales.b: Thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi and does not explain the paired trapezius signs.
rationales.d: Dorsal scapular nerve affects rhomboids, but trapezius denervation best accounts for shoulder droop plus winging here.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q004.takeaway: Teres major is outside the SITS rotator cuff; teres minor, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and subscapularis stabilize the joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q004.displayText: Teres major is not a rotator-cuff muscle. The rotator cuff is the SITS group: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis; these muscles stabilize the shoulder.

rationales.a: Teres minor is one of the four rotator-cuff muscles.
rationales.c: Infraspinatus is part of the SITS cuff and externally rotates/stabilizes the humeral head.
rationales.d: Subscapularis is the anterior rotator-cuff component.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q006.takeaway: Latissimus dorsi, via thoracodorsal nerve, extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm; its nerve is at risk in axillary surgery.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q006.displayText:
Latissimus dorsi is most likely affected. It is innervated by the thoracodorsal nerve, which may be injured during radical mastectomy.

Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm.
emphasis: Latissimus dorsi is most likely affected

rationales.b: Teres minor laterally rotates the arm and is supplied by axillary nerve.
rationales.d: Pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates but does not provide the full extension action specified.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q007.takeaway: Pectoralis major is not an overhead-abduction muscle; serratus anterior and trapezius rotate the scapula after deltoid/supraspinatus initiate elevation.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q007.displayText:
Pectoralis major mainly adducts and medially rotates the arm and is not involved in shoulder abduction.

The first 15 degrees of abduction is initiated by supraspinatus; approximately 15-90 degrees is carried mainly by the middle deltoid; beyond 90 degrees, rotation of the shoulder girdle by trapezius and serratus anterior contributes.

rationales.a: Serratus anterior assists upward scapular rotation for elevation above shoulder level.
rationales.b: Deltoid contributes strongly to arm abduction through the middle range.
rationales.c: Trapezius rotates the scapula to permit overhead abduction.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q008.takeaway: The Popeye bulge after heavy lifting is characteristic of proximal long-head biceps tendon rupture, with distal muscle retraction.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q008.displayText:
The image shows the Popeye sign, classically seen with proximal biceps tendon rupture. The bulge becomes prominent on elbow flexion as the unrestrained muscle fibres contract.

Proximal biceps tendon rupture makes up the large majority of biceps tendon ruptures and often has little effect on overall upper-limb function but produces the characteristic deformity.

The source notes common tendon-rupture sites including quadriceps, Achilles, rotator cuff (especially supraspinatus), and biceps.
emphasis: The image shows the Popeye sign, classically seen with proximal biceps tendon rupture
The bulge becomes prominent on elbow flexion as the unrestrained muscle fibres contract
Proximal biceps tendon rupture makes up the large majority of biceps tendon ruptures and often has little effect on overall upper-limb function but produces the characteristic deformity

rationales.a: Brachialis is an elbow flexor but its tendon rupture does not produce the biceps Popeye deformity.
rationales.b: Distal biceps rupture affects supination/flexion and changes the antecubital contour; the characteristic bulge described is proximal rupture.
rationales.d: The muscle belly itself is not the usual tendon rupture site producing the classic Popeye sign.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q009.takeaway: Biceps brachii and the long head of triceps each cross both shoulder and elbow; the short head of triceps does not cross the shoulder.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q009.displayText: The long head of triceps and biceps brachii cross both the shoulder and elbow joints and therefore act at both joints.
emphasis: The long head of triceps and biceps brachii cross both the shoulder and elbow joints and therefore act at both joints

rationales.a: Brachialis crosses only the elbow, so this pair does not both cross the shoulder.
rationales.b: Coracobrachialis crosses the shoulder but terminates on the humerus before the elbow.
rationales.c: Brachialis again fails to cross the shoulder, despite the long head of triceps doing so.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q010.takeaway: Musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, supplies it, and continues to the anterior arm flexors.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q010.displayText: The nerve shown is the musculocutaneous nerve. In the axilla it pierces coracobrachialis, innervates it, and then passes through the muscle into the arm to supply the anterior arm muscles including biceps brachii and brachialis.

rationales.a: Short-head biceps is supplied by musculocutaneous nerve but is not the muscle it pierces.
rationales.b: Long-head biceps tendon passes through the shoulder joint and bicipital groove; it is not pierced by the nerve.
rationales.d: Medial-head triceps is a posterior-arm muscle supplied by radial nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q011.takeaway: Biceps brachii inserts on the radial tuberosity, the raised area marked on the proximal radius.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q011.displayText:
The image shows the radius, identified by the radial head. The marked raised area is the radial tuberosity, which receives the insertion of biceps brachii.

The short head of biceps arises from the coracoid process and the long head from the supraglenoid tubercle; both unite into a tendon that inserts on the radial tuberosity. Innervation is by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6).

rationales.c: Brachioradialis inserts near the distal radius at the styloid region.
rationales.d: Long-head triceps inserts on the olecranon of the ulna.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q013.takeaway: Extensor carpi radialis longus branches from radial nerve before deep-branch continuation as posterior interosseous nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q013.displayText:
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brachioradialis are supplied by the radial nerve before it divides into superficial and deep branches.

After the deep branch of the radial nerve penetrates supinator it is called the posterior interosseous nerve, which supplies the remaining extrinsic wrist/finger extensors except extensor carpi radialis longus.

rationales.a: Extensor carpi ulnaris is supplied by posterior interosseous nerve.
rationales.c: Extensor digitorum is supplied by posterior interosseous nerve.
rationales.d: Extensor digiti minimi is supplied by posterior interosseous nerve.
